content: The Harvard Atherosclerosis Reversibility Project (HARP) was designed to investigate the impact of intensive lipid-lowering therapy on the progression of atherosclerosis in patients with normal cholesterol levels. Specifically, the study aimed to determine whether such therapy could influence the angiographic progression of coronary atherosclerosis. HARP was conducted as a randomized, placebo-controlled trial. A total of 91 patients with normal cholesterol levels, defined as having total serum cholesterol concentrations below 250 mg/dL, were enrolled. These participants underwent a stepwise treatment regimen that included dietary modifications, followed by the administration of pravastatin, nicotinic acid, cholestyramine, and gemfibrozil over a period of 2.5 years. To evaluate the effects of the treatment, coronary angiograms were performed at baseline and repeated after the treatment period to assess changes in coronary atherosclerosis. The results of the study demonstrated significant improvements in lipid profiles, including reductions in total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels, as well as an increase in high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) levels. Despite these favorable changes in lipid parameters, the repeat coronary angiograms did not reveal significant differences in the degree of coronary artery obstruction, the progression of coronary stenosis, or the regression of atherosclerotic lesions. Additionally, there were no significant differences in the incidence of clinical cardiac events between the treatment and placebo groups. In conclusion, the findings of this study indicate that intensive lipid-lowering therapy does not significantly alter the rate of progression of coronary stenoses in patients with normal cholesterol levels.
